DETAILED: Here's a realistic filing scenario: You receive folders for Santos, Santiago, and Santillan. All share S-a-n-t, so you must compare further. The fifth letters are o, i, i. Since 'i' comes before 'o', Santiago and Santillan precede Santos. Between Santiago and Santillan, compare the next differing letters: a vs l. Since 'a' comes before 'l', the final order is Santiago, Santillan, Santos.

Consider filing applications in a DILG office: Clerk, Clear, Clearance. Compare letter by letter: C-l-e matches for all three. Fourth letters: r (Clerk), a (Clear), a (Clearance). Since 'a' comes before 'r', both Clear and Clearance precede Clerk. Between Clear and Clearance: Clear ends at position 5, while Clearance continues. The shorter word comes first, giving us: Clear, Clearance, Clerk.

A practical example from a COA office: You need to file records for Data, Database, and Date. D-a-t matches for all three. Fourth letters: a (Data), a (Database), e (Date). Since 'a' comes before 'e', Data and Database precede Date. Between Data and Database, Data is shorter and all compared letters match, so Data comes first. Final order: Data, Database, Date.

In a government payroll office, you're filing: Mendoza, Mercado, Mercado Jr. Compare: M-e matches for all. Third letters: n (Mendoza), r (Mercado), r (Mercado Jr.). Since 'n' comes before 'r', Mendoza is first. Between Mercado and Mercado Jr., Mercado is shorter with all letters matching the longer version, so Mercado comes before Mercado Jr. Final order: Mendoza, Mercado, Mercado Jr.

Filing correspondence from different agencies: Agency, Agenda, Agreement. A-g matches for all. Third letters: e (Agency), e (Agenda), r (Agreement). Since 'e' comes before 'r', Agency and Agenda precede Agreement. Between Agency and Agenda: fourth letters are n vs n. Fifth letters: c vs d. Since 'c' comes before 'd', Agency comes before Agenda. Final order: Agency, Agenda, Agreement.

STANDARD: Scanning technique: Point to the first letter of each word. Find the earliest. If tied, move to the second letter. Repeat until the tie breaks. The 'finger-tracking method' prevents skipping letters.

Checklist approach: (1) Compare first letters — different? Done. (2) Same first letter? Compare second. (3) Still tied? Keep going letter by letter. (4) One word ends while matching? Shorter word first.
Remember the alphabet in chunks: A-F, G-L, M-R, S-Z. When you see a letter, instantly know which chunk it belongs to. This speeds up mental comparison without reciting the full alphabet.
Use elimination: find the entry that definitely comes FIRST (earliest initial letter), mark it, then compare the remaining entries. This reduces the comparison workload step by step.
Memory phrase: 'Spell it, don't say it.' Alphabetizing uses exact spelling, never pronunciation. If you catch yourself sounding out words, stop and look at the actual letters instead.
DETAILED: Multi-step scanning system: (1) Scan all first letters — group entries by initial. (2) For same-initial groups, move to second letter. (3) Continue position by position until differences emerge. (4) Apply shorter-word rule when one entry ends while all letters match. (5) Use alphabet chunking (A-F, G-L, M-R, S-Z) for quick position recall. This systematic approach prevents the most common exam error: jumping ahead without checking earlier positions.

The 'letter ladder' visualization: imagine climbing a ladder where each rung is a letter position. You climb both words simultaneously. The moment one word's rung is lower (earlier in alphabet), that word goes first. If one ladder ends while matching, the shorter ladder wins. This mental model makes multi-letter comparison intuitive.

Finger-tracking method for exam day: (1) Place your finger under the first letter of each option. (2) Identify the earliest — that's your answer for position 1. (3) Among remaining entries, repeat for position 2. Key rule: never skip to later letters without confirming earlier ones match. For commonly confused pairs (M/N, P/Q, U/V), verify by mentally reciting the 3-letter neighborhood.

Compare second letters carefully (this is where most errors happen with names like Baker/Black/Brown). CHECK 3 — Multiple letters match? Use the 'finished first, filed first' rule for length differences. This covers the three question types the exam uses most frequently.

Speed technique combined with accuracy: Break comparison into phases. Phase 1 (instant): Different first letters — rank by alphabet chunk. Phase 2 (5 seconds): Same first letter — compare positions 2-3. Phase 3 (10 seconds): Deep match — letter-by-letter through position 4+. Most exam questions resolve in Phase 1 or 2. SIMPLIFIED: To alphabetize: compare first letters. If same, compare second letters. Keep going until you find a difference.

STANDARD: Arranging words alphabetically follows a systematic process: (1) Compare first letters. (2) If first letters match, compare second letters. (3) Continue comparing letter by letter until a difference appears. (4) The word with the earlier letter at the point of difference goes first.

The method is sequential comparison. Start at position 1. If letters match, advance to position 2. Keep advancing until you find a mismatch. At the mismatch, the word with the alphabetically earlier letter takes priority. This works for any pair of words regardless of length.

Think of it as a decision tree: each letter position is a decision point. Same letter? Move to the next position. Different letters? Decision made — earlier letter wins. This process always terminates because eventually letters will differ (or one word will end).

The arrangement rule is straightforward: left-to-right comparison until a difference emerges. For 'Ball, Cat, Dog' — first letters B, C, D are all different, so one comparison step gives you the order. For words sharing initial letters, you simply extend the comparison deeper.

Alphabetizing is resolved by the first point of difference between entries. Compare letter 1 of each word. If they differ, you have your answer. If they match, compare letter 2. The process continues until a difference determines the order.
DETAILED: The systematic arrangement process has four steps: (1) Compare first letters of all entries. (2) If first letters match for some entries, compare their second letters. (3) Continue comparing additional letters one by one until every entry can be distinguished. (4) At each comparison point, the entry with the alphabetically earlier letter ranks higher. This process handles any number of entries and any word length, because it always terminates at either a letter difference or a word boundary.

The section teaches the core algorithm of alphabetizing. It's important to understand that this is a SEQUENTIAL process — you cannot skip to position 3 without confirming positions 1 and 2 match. This sequential discipline prevents the most common exam error (jumping ahead). The examples (Ball/Cat/Dog and Mango/Apple/Orange) demonstrate both the simple case (different first letters) and reordering based on letter positions.

The arrangement method works through positional comparison: Position 1 first, then Position 2 if needed, then Position 3, and so on. This is essentially the same algorithm computers use for sorting strings. For humans under exam pressure, the key discipline is: never skip a position. If you compare positions 1, 2, 3 and they all match, you MUST check position 4 — not jump to position 6 because it 'looks' different.

Two examples illustrate different difficulty levels: (1) Ball, Cat, Dog — first letters B, C, D are all distinct, so comparison resolves at position 1. This represents the easiest exam question type. (2) Mango, Apple, Orange — first letters M, A, O are distinct but NOT in the given order. You must recognize that A(1) < M(13) < O(15) to reorder them as Apple, Mango, Orange. The second example tests both comparison skill and reordering ability.

The four-step process is the universal algorithm for alphabetizing any set of entries. Step 1 (first letters) resolves entries with different initials. Step 2 (second letters) resolves entries sharing the same initial. Steps 3-4 (continuing comparison) handle the most complex cases where multiple positions match. Every exam question, regardless of apparent difficulty, is solved by applying these four steps systematically and without shortcuts.

Reyes, Cruz, Santos — R, C, S. C < R < S. Filed as: Cruz, Reyes, Santos.
Budget, Personnel, Accounting — B, P, A. A < B < P. Order: Accounting, Budget, Personnel.

STANDARD: Example 1: Ball, Cat, Dog. Compare first letters: B(2), C(3), D(4). Since 2 < 3 < 4, the order is Ball, Cat, Dog — resolved with one comparison at position 1. This is the simplest case.

Mixed case: Given Budget, Benefits, Billing. First letters: B, B, B — all same! This tells you position 1 doesn't resolve it. You'd need to move to position 2 (u, e, i). Since e < i < u: Benefits, Billing, Budget. This bridges into the next section on second-letter comparison.
DETAILED: Detailed walkthrough of Example 2 (Mango, Apple, Orange): Step 1 — Extract first letters: M, A, O. Step 2 — Determine alphabet positions: M=13, A=1, O=15. Step 3 — Sort by position: A(1) < M(13) < O(15). Step 4 — Map back to words: Apple(A), Mango(M), Orange(O). Final answer: Apple, Mango, Orange. Total comparisons needed: just 1 (at position 1). Complex office scenario: A DILG office receives correspondence from 5 agencies — TESDA(T), CHED(C), DepEd(D), DSWD(D), CSC(C). Step 1: First letters T, C, D, D, C. Step 2: Group by first letter — C group: CHED, CSC. D group: DepEd, DSWD. T group: TESDA. Step 3: Order groups: C first, D second, T third. Step 4: Within C group, compare second letters: H vs S. H(8) < S(19), so CHED before CSC. Within D group: e vs S. Lowercase e = E(5), S(19), so DepEd before DSWD. Final: CHED, CSC, DepEd, DSWD, TESDA.

Step 2: Sort positions: A(1), F(6), L(12), P(16). Step 3: Final answer: Administration, Finance, Logistics, Procurement. This resolves entirely at position 1 — a 20-second answer for a prepared examinee.

Multi-step example showing process discipline: Given 'Castro, Cruz, Cabrera, Chavez.' All start with C — position 1 doesn't resolve anything. Move to position 2: a(1), r(18), a(1), h(8). Group by position 2: 'a' group (Castro, Cabrera) at position 1, then 'h' group (Chavez) at position 8, then 'r' group (Cruz) at position 18. Within 'a' group, move to position 3: s(19) vs b(2). B < S, so Cabrera before Castro. Final: Cabrera, Castro, Chavez, Cruz.

Realistic government filing exercise: You receive forms from Reyes, Maria; Reyes, Jose; Rivera, Ana; Ramos, Pedro. Step 1: All start with R — move to position 2: e, e, i, a. Since a(1) < e(5) < i(9): Ramos first. Between the two 'e' entries (Reyes, Maria and Reyes, Jose): move to position 3: y=y. Position 4: e=e. Position 5: s=s. They match through the surname! In practice, you'd then compare first names: Jose(J=10) vs Maria(M=13), so Reyes, Jose before Reyes, Maria. Final: Ramos Pedro, Reyes Jose, Reyes Maria, Rivera Ana.

Compare. Same? Both slide right. Different? The one under the alphabetically earlier letter wins. STANDARD: First-letter comparison is the simplest alphabetizing technique: when entries begin with different letters, the one with the alphabetically earlier first letter comes first. No further comparison is needed. This resolves most straightforward filing tasks immediately.

The first letter acts as the primary sorting category. Santos(S), Reyes(R), Cruz(C) — compare first letters S, R, C. Since C < R < S in the alphabet, the order is Cruz, Reyes, Santos. One comparison step, done.

When first letters differ, they serve as complete sorting keys. Budget(B), Accounting(A), Personnel(P) — first letters B, A, P sort as A < B < P, giving Accounting, Budget, Personnel. This is the fastest resolution possible.

First-letter comparison works because the initial letter narrows records into one of 26 groups. When entries are in different groups, the groups themselves determine order. Only when entries share the same group (same first letter) do you need deeper comparison.

The principle: first letters that differ resolve the comparison immediately. The exam includes many questions at this level — they're designed to be answered quickly. The key is confidence in letter positions so you don't second-guess.
DETAILED: First-letter comparison is the base case of the alphabetizing algorithm: when the first letters of entries differ, those letters alone determine the complete ordering. No second-letter comparison is needed. The section demonstrates this with two examples: Santos/Reyes/Cruz (S > R > C, so order is Cruz, Reyes, Santos) and Budget/Accounting/Personnel (B > A but B < P, so order is Accounting, Budget, Personnel). Both resolve in a single comparison step.

The section explains WHY first-letter comparison works beyond just HOW: the first letter acts as a primary sorting category. By grouping entries by initial letter, large collections are immediately divided into 26 sections. This is the fundamental efficiency of alphabetical filing — finding a record starting with 'M' in a system of 1000 records means searching approximately 38 records (1000/26) rather than all 1000.

First-letter comparison also carries an important misconception alert: words that START with the same SOUND are NOT alphabetized together. 'Phone' and 'Folder' both start with an 'F' sound, but Phone(P) comes after Folder(F) alphabetically because comparison uses spelling, not pronunciation. This distinction between sound-based and letter-based grouping is a common exam trap.

The section establishes a critical principle: alphabetizing depends on EXACT SPELLING, not pronunciation. This is demonstrated by the misconception example where 'Phone' and 'Folder' are NOT grouped together despite sharing a phonetic initial. Chunk-based comparison shortcut: know your alphabet groups (A-F, G-L, M-R, S-Z). Different chunks = instant ranking without counting exact positions. Same chunk = briefly verify within the 6-letter group. This reduces mental load from 26 possible positions to 4 groups.

Long-term memory for pronunciation traps: create a 'rogues gallery' of letters that misbehave phonetically. The Ph(=P not F), Kn(=K not N), Wr(=W not R), Ps(=P not S), Pn(=P not N) family. Two key examples demonstrate the range of second-letter comparison: (1) Baker/Black/Brown — English words where second letters (a, l, r) are well-separated in the alphabet. Easy to compare. Automaticity drill: Create a deck of cards with Filipino surname sets sharing initials. Shuffle and draw one card per day. Immediately sort by second letter and time yourself. The shorter-word rule is critical here: when one word ends while all its letters match the longer word, the shorter word comes first. Clear comes before Clearance because Clear ends at position 5 while Clearance continues — and all compared letters matched perfectly.

Multi-letter comparison requires patience and precision. Santos/Santiago/Santillan need comparison through position 5 to resolve. This is the hardest type of alphabetizing question because it demands tracking multiple positions without error.

Two scenarios arise in multi-letter comparison: (1) A difference eventually appears (Santos vs Santiago at position 5: o vs i). (2) One word is a prefix of another (Clear vs Clearance — Clear is entirely contained in Clearance). Rule: difference → earlier letter wins. Prefix → shorter word wins.

The section's key insight: 'Shorter words come first when all compared letters are identical.' This is NOT the same as 'shorter words always come first.' It only applies when the shorter word is a prefix of the longer one — like Data/Database or File/Filing.
DETAILED: Multi-letter comparison extends the algorithm past position 2 for entries with multiple matching initial letters. The section demonstrates with two detailed examples: (1) Santos/Santiago/Santillan — matching through S-a-n-t, differentiating at position 5 (o vs i vs i), then further resolving Santiago/Santillan at position 6 (a vs l). (2) Clerk/Clearance/Clear — matching through C-l-e, differentiating at position 4 (r vs a vs a), then applying the shorter-word rule between Clear and Clearance.

The section introduces the shorter-word rule as a special case: when all compared letters are identical up to the end of one word, the shorter word comes first. This is formalized as 'Finished first, filed first.' Important misconception: 'Longer words always come later' is FALSE. 'Clear' comes before 'Clearance' (shorter word is prefix), but 'Clerk' comes AFTER both (different letter at position 4). Length only matters when one word is an exact prefix of another.

Multi-letter comparison is where most exam errors occur because it requires sustained attention across multiple positions. The cognitive load increases with each matching position — at position 5 or 6, working memory is stretched. The section's examples deliberately use Filipino surnames (Santos/Santiago/Santillan) because these commonly share long prefixes, making deep comparison a realistic government filing scenario.

The section addresses a common misconception: 'Longer words always come later.' This is wrong. Length only matters when the shorter word is entirely contained within the longer word (prefix relationship). If words differ at some position, length is irrelevant — the letter difference determines order regardless of remaining length. Clear(5 letters) before Clearance(9 letters) = shorter-word rule. Clear(5 letters) before Clerk(5 letters) = letter comparison (a < r at position 4).

Two algorithmic rules govern multi-letter comparison: Rule 1 (standard): keep comparing until a letter difference appears, then rank by that difference. Rule 2 (shorter-word): if one word ends while all its letters match the other word exactly, the ended word comes first. These two rules, combined with the position-by-position approach, handle every possible comparison. No additional rules are needed for any case the exam presents.

SIMPLIFIED: Santos, Santiago, Santillan — match through S-a-n-t. Fifth letters: o, i, i. i < o, so Santiago and Santillan first.
Clear, Clearance, Clerk — fourth letters: a, a, r. Clear/Clearance beat Clerk. Then Clear beats Clearance (shorter word rule).
Data, Database — Data ends while matching Database. Shorter word first: Data before Database.

STANDARD: Example 1: Santos/Santiago/Santillan. Compare: S=S=S, a=a=a, n=n=n, t=t=t. Position 5: o(Santos), i(Santiago), i(Santillan). Since i < o, both Santiago and Santillan come before Santos. Between Santiago and Santillan: position 6 is a vs l. Since a < l, Santiago before Santillan. Final: Santiago, Santillan, Santos.

Example 2: Clerk/Clearance/Clear. Compare: C=C=C, l=l=l, e=e=e. Position 4: r(Clerk), a(Clearance), a(Clear). Since a < r, Clear and Clearance come before Clerk. Between Clear and Clearance: Clear ends at position 5 while Clearance continues. Shorter word first: Clear before Clearance. Final: Clear, Clearance, Clerk.

Shorter-word example: Data vs Database. Compare: D=D, a=a, t=t, a=a. Data ends at position 4 while Database continues. All compared letters match perfectly, so the shorter word (Data) comes first. Order: Data, Database.

Filipino name example: Mercado vs Mercedes. Compare: M=M, e=e, r=r, c=c. Position 5: a(Mercado) vs e(Mercedes). Since a < e, Mercado comes before Mercedes. Note: this resolves by letter difference, NOT by the shorter-word rule.

Government filing: Cabinet vs Cable. Compare: C=C, a=a, b=b. Position 4: i(Cabinet) vs l(Cable). Since i < l, Cabinet comes before Cable. Deep comparison needed even for short words when they share a common prefix.
DETAILED: Full step-by-step for Santos/Santiago/Santillan: Position 1: S=S=S (match). Position 2: a=a=a (match). Position 3: n=n=n (match). Position 4: t=t=t (match). Position 5: o(Santos), i(Santiago), i(Santillan) — DIFFERENCE FOUND. i < o, so Santiago and Santillan precede Santos. Now resolve Santiago vs Santillan: Position 6: a(Santiago) vs l(Santillan). a < l, so Santiago precedes Santillan. Final order: Santiago, Santillan, Santos. Required: comparison through position 6.

Full step-by-step for Clerk/Clearance/Clear: Position 1: C=C=C. Position 2: l=l=l. Position 3: e=e=e. Position 4: r(Clerk), a(Clearance), a(Clear) — DIFFERENCE. a < r, so both 'Clea-' entries precede Clerk. Resolve Clear vs Clearance: Position 5: r(Clear)=r(Clearance). Clear ends at position 5. Clearance continues: a-n-c-e. Since Clear is a prefix of Clearance (all letters match until Clear ends), SHORTER WORD FIRST. Final: Clear, Clearance, Clerk. Two rules applied: letter comparison (a < r) and shorter-word rule.

Complex real scenario: Filing records for Cabrera, Caballero, Cabinet, Cable. All share C-a-b. Position 4: r(Cabrera), a(Caballero), i(Cabinet), l(Cable). Sort position 4: a(1) < i(9) < l(12) < r(18). Order: Caballero, Cabinet, Cable, Cabrera. Note how deep comparison (position 4) was needed despite all entries being common Filipino/English words. The exam includes exactly this type of set.

Exam-style compound problem: Arrange: Agency, Agenda, Agreement. All share A-g. Position 3: e(Agency, Agenda), r(Agreement). Since e < r, Agency and Agenda precede Agreement. Resolve Agency vs Agenda: Position 4: n(Agency), n(Agenda). Match. Position 5: c(Agency), d(Agenda). c < d, so Agency before Agenda. Final: Agency, Agenda, Agreement. Required comparison through position 5 for full resolution.

The shorter-word rule in government filing context: Mercado vs 'Mercado Jr.' — the surname 'Mercado' is entirely contained in 'Mercado Jr.' After position 7 (o), Mercado ends while 'Mercado Jr.' continues. All compared letters matched, so shorter entry (Mercado) files before longer entry (Mercado Jr.). This pattern appears in real government files where employees share surnames with different suffixes (Jr., Sr., III).

STANDARD: The 'Finished first, filed first' mnemonic handles the shorter-word rule perfectly. When one word runs out of letters while matching the other word: the finished (shorter) word gets filed first. Say it before each multi-letter comparison question.

Position-tracking technique: write the comparison position number above each letter as you compare. Position 1, 2, 3, 4... When you find the difference, circle that number. This physical tracking prevents the most common error: losing your place during deep comparison.

Two-rule framework: multi-letter comparison has exactly two possible outcomes. OUTCOME A: you find a letter difference → rank by that letter. OUTCOME B: one word ends while matching → shorter word first. Before answering, verify which outcome you're using. If it's B, double-check that ALL previous letters actually matched.

Practice with 'San-' surnames: Santos, Santiago, Santillan, Sanchez, Sandoval. These share S-a-n and require comparison at position 4+. Practice sorting this specific set until automatic, because the exam frequently uses exactly this pattern with Filipino San- names.

Error prevention: after determining your answer for a multi-letter question, ask: 'Did I apply the right rule?' If one word is shorter: 'Did ALL letters match?' If yes → shorter first. If no → the letter difference determines order, not length. This self-check catches the most common multi-letter comparison mistake.
DETAILED: Build a 'deep comparison checklist' for exam day: (1) Identify the shared prefix length (how many positions match). (2) Write down the first differing position. (3) If one word ends: verify ALL previous positions match, then apply shorter-word rule. (4) If letters differ: rank by the differing letters. (5) Verify: does your answer change if you check one more position? This 5-step checklist catches 95% of multi-letter errors.

Kinesthetic memory for the shorter-word rule: hold up your left hand (5 fingers = 'Data,' 4 letters + stop). Hold up your right hand (8 fingers = 'Database,' 8 letters). The hand that runs out of fingers first goes first in filing. Physically acting this out during practice sessions encodes the rule in procedural memory, making it retrievable under exam stress.

Create a practice set specifically for multi-letter mastery: (1) San-group: Santos, Santiago, Santillan, Sanchez, Sandoval. (2) Clear-group: Clear, Clearance, Clerk, Client. Long-term encoding for the shorter-word rule distinction: create two visual categories. Category 1 ('Prefix case' — shorter word rule applies): Data/Database, File/Filing, Clear/Clearance. Visualize these as Russian nesting dolls — the smaller one fits perfectly inside the larger one. Category 2 ('Difference case' — letter comparison applies): Clerk/Clear, Mendoza/Mercado, Santos/Santiago. Visualize these as different-colored blocks that don't nest. The visual distinction between 'nesting' and 'different colors' instantly tells you which rule to apply.

The section identifies four commonly confused letter positions: E and I (vowels separated by 4 positions but mentally grouped), M and N (adjacent mid-alphabet letters often swapped), P and Q (Q is rare in Filipino names, causing position uncertainty), U and V (visually similar and adjacent). SIMPLIFIED: Is M before N? Yes. (Adjacent pair — memorize this.) Is P before R? Yes. P is in M-R chunk, before R.
Quick: G or L first? G. Both in G-L chunk, G starts the chunk. No counting needed.
E or I? E comes first. Remember: E(5) before I(9). Both vowels, but E is earlier.
U or V? U comes first. They're adjacent and in order — U(21), V(22). Just like the alphabet song.
T or S? S comes first. S(19) before T(20). S-Z chunk: S starts it, T follows.
STANDARD: Chunk comparison example: Is M before G? M is in chunk 3 (M-R), G is in chunk 2 (G-L). Chunk 2 < chunk 3, so G comes first. Resolved without knowing exact positions (G=7, M=13).

Within-chunk comparison: Baker vs Brown. Both start with B (chunk 1: A-F). Second letters: a vs r. Both 'a' and 'r' are in different chunks (a=chunk 1, r=chunk 3). Chunk 1 < chunk 3, so 'a' comes first → Baker before Brown.
Confused pair resolution: Mercado vs Navarro. First letters M and N. These are commonly confused adjacent letters. Remember the sequence: L-M-N. M comes before N. So Mercado before Navarro.

Speed application: sorting Personnel, Quarterly, Monthly, Audit. First letters: P(chunk 3), Q(chunk 3), M(chunk 3), A(chunk 1). Immediately: A (chunk 1) is first. Among P, Q, M (all chunk 3): M < P < Q. Final: Audit, Monthly, Personnel, Quarterly.

The E/I confusion in practice: comparing 'Services' and 'Signature.' Second letters: e and i. These vowels confuse people. Remember A-E-I-O-U order: E(position 5) before I(position 9). So Services before Signature.
DETAILED: Full demonstration of chunk-based speed: Given entries Tarlac(T), Bulacan(B), Quezon(Q), Manila(M), Isabela(I). Step 1: Classify by chunk. B=chunk1, I=chunk2, M=chunk3, Q=chunk3, T=chunk4. STANDARD: Four speed techniques for faster alphabetizing: (1) Compare only until a difference appears — don't analyze every letter unnecessarily. (2) Focus on the first three letters where most differences occur. (3) Ignore capitalization entirely — it has no effect on alphabetical order. (4) Use elimination — find the earliest entry first, remove it, then find the next earliest.

Technique 1 is the biggest time-saver: once you find where entries differ, STOP comparing. You have your answer. Continuing to compare later letters wastes time without changing the result. For Cruz vs Castro, the difference is at position 2 (r vs a) — no need to look at positions 3, 4, 5.

Technique 4 (elimination) is especially useful for ordering 4-5 entries: instead of trying to determine all positions simultaneously, find which entry is FIRST, set it aside, then find which of the remaining is next. This breaks a complex problem into simple pairwise comparisons.

Technique 3 (ignore capitalization) prevents a common hesitation: some examinees wonder if 'Garcia' and 'garcia' alphabetize differently. They don't. Case is irrelevant in alphabetical filing. This eliminates a false decision point that wastes time.

These techniques optimize the systematic comparison process for speed without sacrificing accuracy. They don't change HOW you compare — they change how efficiently you do it by eliminating unnecessary steps.
DETAILED: The section presents four efficiency optimizations for the alphabetizing algorithm: Technique 1 (early termination) — stop comparing the moment a difference appears. All subsequent letters are irrelevant to ordering. This alone can save 5-10 seconds on entries with long post-difference tails. Technique 2 (front-loading attention) — statistically, most differences appear within the first 3 letters. Allocate more attention to positions 1-3 and less to positions 4+.

Technique 3 (case-insensitivity) eliminates a false variable. Alphabetical filing is case-insensitive: 'Garcia' = 'garcia' = 'GARCIA'. Some examinees waste time wondering about this, especially when entries have inconsistent capitalization. The rule is absolute: case never affects filing order. This also means acronyms (CSC, DILG) alphabetize the same as full words starting with those letters.

Technique 4 (elimination/greedy approach) restructures the ordering problem. Instead of determining all positions simultaneously (complex), find the FIRST entry (simple pairwise comparison), remove it, then find the FIRST of the remaining set, and repeat. This greedy approach converts an n-entry ordering problem into n-1 'find the minimum' problems, each of which is cognitively simpler.

The four techniques address different efficiency bottlenecks: Technique 1 addresses post-resolution waste (comparing letters after the answer is determined). Technique 2 addresses attention allocation (directing focus where differences are most likely). Technique 3 addresses false variables (eliminating irrelevant considerations). Technique 4 addresses problem complexity (simplifying multi-entry ordering into sequential minimum-finding).

These speed techniques are optimizations, not replacements for the core algorithm. You still compare left-to-right, still use the shorter-word rule, still rely on exact spelling. What changes is: you stop earlier (Technique 1), focus attention better (Technique 2), ignore irrelevant factors (Technique 3), and decompose complex problems (Technique 4). Together they can reduce average item time from 45 seconds to 25-30 seconds without any accuracy loss.
